title: My Calendar II
description:
# My Calendar II

You are implementing a calendar. A new event may be booked only when adding it does not create a **triple booking**.

A **triple booking** happens when three accepted events all cover at least one common time point. Each event is represented by a half-open interval `[start, end)`, meaning every time `x` with `start <= x < end`. Two events that only touch at an endpoint do not overlap at that endpoint.

The calendar may contain double-booked time ranges, but no time point may be covered by three events.

Implement the `MyCalendarTwo` class:

*   `MyCalendarTwo()` initializes an empty calendar.
*   `boolean book(int start, int end)` returns `true` and stores the event if it can be added without a triple booking. Otherwise it returns `false` and must leave the calendar unchanged.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["MyCalendarTwo", "book", "book", "book", "book", "book", "book"]
[[], [10, 20], [50, 60], [10, 40], [5, 15], [5, 10], [25, 55]]
**Output**
[null, true, true, true, false, true, true]
**Explanation**
`[10, 20)`, `[50, 60)`, and `[10, 40)` are accepted. `[5, 15)` is rejected because `[10, 15)` would be covered by three events. `[5, 10)` is accepted because it only touches the double-booked range at `10`. `[25, 55)` is accepted because every point in that range is covered by at most two events.

## Constraints:

*   `0 <= start < end <= 10^9`
*   At most `1000` calls will be made to `book`.

examples.output: [null, true, true, true, false, true, true]

solutions.name: Single and Double Booking Lists
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain one list of all accepted bookings and another list of ranges that are already double-booked. A new event is invalid if it overlaps any double-booked range. Otherwise, compute its overlap with every accepted booking, append each non-empty overlap to the double-booked list, and then store the event.

## Key Insight

The double-booked list is an explicit record of dangerous ranges. Any future overlap with one of those ranges would create a triple booking, while overlaps with single-booked ranges merely create new double-booked ranges.

## Complexity Analysis

Each booking scans the current single and double lists, so it costs O(n). In the worst case there can be O(n^2) recorded double-booked ranges across all calls.

solutions.name: TreeMap Sweep-Line with Rollback
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a `TreeMap` of sweep-line deltas: add `+1` at each start and `-1` at each end. For a tentative booking, apply the two deltas, scan the active count in time order, and reject if the count reaches three. On rejection, undo both tentative deltas.

## Key Insight

The sweep-line count is exactly the number of active events at each time segment. The rollback step is part of correctness because a failed `book` call must not leave hidden state behind.

## Complexity Analysis

Each attempt updates O(log n) endpoints and scans O(n) distinct endpoints. The map uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Dynamic Segment Tree Max Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a dynamic lazy segment tree over `[0, 10^9]`. Query the maximum booking count on `[start, end - 1]`; if it is already at least two, adding the new event would create a triple booking. Otherwise add one to the whole range.

## Key Insight

This is a range-add, range-maximum problem over a huge coordinate domain. The tree stores only touched nodes, and queries must carry ancestor lazy values even when a child node has not been created yet.

## Complexity Analysis

Each query and update costs O(log U), where `U = 10^9 + 1`. Every successful booking may allocate O(log U) nodes, so worst-case space is O(n log U).

solutions.name: Coordinate Compression Rebuild
solutions.description:
## Approach

Tentatively append the new event, collect all current start and end coordinates, sort them, and examine each elementary segment between adjacent coordinates. Count how many accepted events cover that segment. If any segment is covered by three events, remove the tentative event and reject it.

## Key Insight

The booking count only changes at event endpoints. Rebuilding compressed segments is slower than the online structures, but it makes the half-open interval model explicit and is a reliable correctness baseline for small call counts.

## Complexity Analysis

There are O(n) endpoints and O(n) elementary segments. Counting coverage by scanning all events gives O(n^2) after sorting endpoints, with O(n) extra space.

solutions.name: Ordered Disjoint Segment Counts
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a `TreeMap` whose keys are segment starts and whose values are the booking count for the half-open segment from that key to the next key. Before processing `[start, end)`, split the map at both boundaries. Then scan only segments inside the new interval; reject if any already has count two, otherwise increment them.

## Key Insight

Splitting at every booking boundary turns overlapping intervals into disjoint elementary segments with uniform counts. This preserves the sweep-line idea as mutable interval state instead of recomputing active counts from scratch.

## Complexity Analysis

Splitting and scanning touched segments costs O(n log n) in the worst case, and the map stores O(n) boundaries.
